title: 艺术家与两次死亡杀死了西方游戏开发，但我们能拯救它
content:
Artists Killed Western Game Development, but We Can Still Save It
0
Artists & Two Deaths Killed Western Game Development, but We Can Save It
Business
Nov 17
Written by
Michail Katkoff
by
Phillip Black
, the Game Economist and a co-host of the Deconstructor of Fun podcast.
Gaming used to be the first thing every new technology touched. Real-time 3D graphics, physics simulation, haptic feedback, in-app payments, VR headsets, and yes, even Web3: games were the popularizing use case! Even AI itself was subsidized by 20 years of gamers buying Nvidia graphics cards. Yet we've completely and demonstrably failed to embrace AI... until a turning point in November.
The failure to embrace AI at its onset isn't just a bump in the road; it represents a radical divergence in who is making games, and it explains why Western game development is quickly moving to the Endangered Species List.
There’s something rotten in the state of game development, and Two Deaths in the Family explain why.
We Argue in the West, While the East Ships
Start with the money. AI went from 15% of all venture deal value in 2016 to 83% in the first three quarters of 2026, while AI's share of game investment never broke 12% (PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor and Konvoy). In February 2025, I wrote that
AI in gaming has flopped
: in the 26 months after ChatGPT launched, web3 made more tangible progress in games than AI did. The money followed the mood, and the mood is worse than indifference.
GDC's November 2026 survey of mostly Western developers found 55% think generative AI is harming the industry,
up from 18% in 2024
.1 Among visual and technical artists, 65% said it was harming the industry. 8% said it helps. Only eight percent!
Obviously, these numbers don't reflect these developers' day-to-day workflows; instead, they reflect what political scientists call
"expressive responding
”, which is answering a survey to show which side you're on rather than what you actually do. And on this, there's no better contrast than Eastern development.
Japan's CESA survey of over 1,000 devs found 86% use generative AI at work, with
63.0% using it daily
, while China's Game Publishing Committee survey reported
86.4% of companies apply AI in production
. Hell, Korea is so in that Krafton
bought its own GPU cluster
.
Over and over again, the complaints have come from one discipline, artists, who have organized campaigns to bully and intimidate any public Western defiance of some vague no-GenAI stance. Arc Raiders' Embark embraced AI back when it was called "machine learning," and its infamous
blog post of an enemy unit figuring out its own animations
would be burned in effigy in the modern discourse. We know this because their (small) use of GenAI for voice lines drummed up such outrage that they were bullied into
re-recording AI voice lines
.
Then there's Clair Obscur, what should be a shining example of a small team embracing new technology, only for the Indie Game Awards to
strip its Game of the Year and Debut Game awards
over a few AI-generated placeholder textures that slipped into the launch build. And in November,
19 Independent Games Festival jurors announced they're "declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity."
Any attempt to make fun of the technology has itself become a relic in the span of months, not years. In 2023, we were laughing at an AI-generated Will Smith trying to eat spaghetti.

Now, AI systems pass controlled Turing tests: GPT-4.5, prompted to adopt a humanlike persona, was
judged human 73% of the time
in five-minute conversations, more often than the actual human it was paired with. And the judges handing out creative awards have been fooled too. In July, an AI-generated image
won a photography competition in Hohhot
, before (of course) the art was excluded after an "investigation". Anti-AI crusaders are still holding onto
Call of Duty's 6th finger
, a classic example of
man bites dog
remembrance. Meanwhile, all of the
"human" slop gets a pass
.
AI's mistake was just that, to be called "Artificial" Intelligence. The more useful way to think about AI is as “aggregated intelligence.” We can draw on an enormous amount of accumulated human knowledge to express ourselves in ways we would never have thought possible. AI fills in the middle space between an idea and reality; our taste and choices determine what we make with it. If I tried describing modern AI to someone from 100, 50, or even 10 years ago, I couldn't think of a better way than to call it God's Paintbrush. It has the ability to manifest 3D models, animation, video, sound, music, and text programs, and it all starts with a chat box.
AI objections mirror silly-looking criticisms of DJing and sampling: you're using other people's work, so your contribution doesn't count. Yet choosing what to combine, what to change, and what to leave out is itself creative work. Of course, that isn't a license to plagiarize copyrighted work. At the end of the day, all artists are “trained” on other people’s work. The books, films, music, and games we grew up with are all over what we make.
The copyright disputes are real, but think again if you believe their resolution will put this technology back in the box. Developers still need to decide what they're going to build with the capabilities already in front of them. I'm sorry, but grievance politics is fine, but it's not an effective growth strategy, and that's what the West needs most.
The great irony in all the drama is that AI is finally the technology that puts artists in the driver's seat. It's a tool of freedom, not oppression. No one makes this case better than
AI Denzel Washington
:
“I've spent the last 10 years chasing creative freedom, sick of wasting my energy on other people's projects just for a paycheck, craving the space to make something truly creat
